nodes.name: Feasibility of a Multimodal Lifestyle Intervention Programme for Patients With Ulcerative Colitis: A Single‐Arm Pilot Study
nodes.venue: JCC Plus
nodes.abstract: Plain Language Summary Lifestyle factors, such as exercise, diet and mental health, have shown promise in improving well‐being in people with ulcerative colitis, a chronic inflammatory condition of the large bowel. However, these factors are usually addressed separately in research. Therefore, we explored whether a 24‐week programme combining exercise, personalised dietary advice and psychological support could be implemented in people with ulcerative colitis. Thirty patients took part in the programme. Most participants remained in the study, and three‐quarters were satisfied with the programme. However, maintaining participation across the different components proved challenging. In particular, adherence to the exercise programme was low, whereas adherence to dietary advice was higher. More than half of the participants were eligible for psychological support, but only a quarter of those started the programme. No unexpected safety concerns were observed. Overall, our findings suggest that patients may be interested in a broad lifestyle approach, but that initial interest does not necessarily translate into sustained participation. Therefore, future programmes should focus on making lifestyle interventions more flexible, practical and tailored to individual people.

nodes.name: Pasture area increases livestock rabies risk in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil: a geospatial analysis of neurological syndrome cases (2020–2024)
nodes.venue: Tropical Animal Health and Production
nodes.abstract: Abstract Animal rabies poses a risk to livestock in Brazil due to transmission by hematophagous bats. The Brazilian sanitary surveillance system mandates rabies testing for any livestock exhibiting signs of neurological syndrome. This geospatial, retrospective, longitudinal, observational study analyzed rabies test results for 204 cattle and 56 horses presenting with neurological syndrome in Rio de Janeiro State, Brazil, from 2020 to 2024. We calculated correlations and linear models between rabies results and municipal land-use types, as well the population of herbivores. Most neurological syndrome cases and positive rabies results occurred in cattle. The final linear model for the number of neurological syndrome cases and positive rabies results incorporated pasture area, shrub area and cattle population. Pasture area was positively correlated with higher numbers ( p = 0.011 and p = 0.005, respectively). Larger shrub area was associated with fewer neurological syndrome reports and fewer positive results ( p = 0.009 and p = 0.010, respectively). Greater cattle population showed a negative association with neurological syndrome notifications and positive detections ( p = 0.085 and p = 0.046, respectively).A higher proportion of positive rabies tests was associated with larger pasture areas ( p = 0.019) and with lower equine populations ( p = 0.115). These findings indicate that the lower animal diversity in pasture areas provides few alternative feeding options for Desmodus rotundus besides livestock, leading to more neurological syndrome cases and animal rabies infections. A larger shrub area offer feed alternatives other than cattle to the bats and a larger cattle population dilutes the frequency of bat meals across individuals, reducing both neurological syndrome notifications and positive rabies detections.

nodes.name: Enhance EV station charge and discharge based on deep learning forecasting method incorporating renewable energy sources and multi-objective optimization algorithm
nodes.venue: International Journal of Renewable Energy Development
nodes.abstract: As electric vehicle charging station operations become more common, proper coordination of energy management is necessary to avoid high operational costs and carbon emissions caused by electric vehicle charging requirements, intermittent renewable sources, and fluctuating electricity rates. In this research, a forecast-based optimization methodology is created with the objective of optimizing the charge-discharge management of a renewable-powered electric vehicle charging station system involving photovoltaic generation, wind generation, fuel cells, electric vehicles, and stationary batteries. First, a recurrent neural network is used to predict relevant time series data, such as photovoltaic energy, wind energy, electric vehicle load demand, fuel cell energy production, and electric vehicle energy consumption. These forecasted data are then applied to a bi-objective energy management optimization problem, which is solved using NSGA-II. The objective is to minimize operating cost and emissions while considering power balance, grid energy exchange, and other operational constraints associated with the fuel cell, battery storage system, and electric vehicles. In this study, two scenarios are examined using one month of hourly data; Scenario 1 does not use stationary batteries, whereas Scenario 2 uses them. The forecasting results show robust predictions, with one-hour-ahead values ranging from 0.9162 to 0.9708. The optimization results show that Scenario 2 provides better energy shifting and peak-period support through battery charging and discharging management. Compared with Scenario 1, the operating cost is reduced from $171,833.86 to $160,388.44, and emissions are decreased from 13,485.48 kg to 12,892.23 kg, leading to 6.7% and 4.4% reductions, respectively.

nodes.name: International Journal of Renewable Energy Development
A Semi‐Interpretable Multimodal Model Combining Electronic Health Records and Chest X‐Rays for <scp>COVID</scp> ‐19‐Related Death Prediction
nodes.venue: Expert Systems
nodes.abstract: ABSTRACT Purpose Prognostic models can benefit from integrating heterogeneous data sources. While deep learning‐based multimodal models often improve predictive performance, their limited interpretability remains a barrier to clinical adoption. Moreover, achieving robust generalization with such models typically requires large and diverse datasets, which are not always available in clinical research. This study evaluated whether a late fusion model combining traditional statistical approaches with deep learning models could rival deep learning‐only multimodal models while preserving interpretability to support clinical use. Methods We conducted a retrospective single‐center cohort study of 965 hospitalized patients with laboratory‐confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2 infection who underwent frontal chest X‐ray imaging during hospitalization between March 2020 and January 2022. Of these, 64 (6.6%) died. Structured clinical data and chest X‐ray images were used to predict COVID‐19‐related death. We developed unimodal baseline models and two multimodal approaches: a deep learning‐based joint fusion model and a late fusion model leveraging logistic regression to combine predictions from the best‐performing models for every data modality. Given the limited sample size and class imbalance, performance was evaluated using repeated five‐fold cross validation. Results The late fusion model achieved the best overall performance, with the highest median test AUPRC of 0.363 (IQR 0.271–0.384) across cross validation folds, outperforming unimodal baselines based on structured clinical data or images alone. The late fusion model also outperformed the joint fusion model, achieving, respectively, a 3.1% and 3.6% relative improvement in AUPRC and Brier score on pooled out‐of‐sample predictions and yielding the highest balanced F1‐score. Moreover, it preserved partial interpretability by linking predictions to clinically meaningful variables such as age and comorbidities and enabling image‐based predictions to be traced back to radiographic abnormalities. Conclusions Late fusion models integrating statistical models for clinical data with deep learning for image classification can enhance prognostic performance over unimodal models without fully sacrificing interpretability. In settings with limited data, they may also outperform deep learning‐based joint fusion models. These findings support late fusion as a promising strategy that warrants prospective evaluation and external validation before clinical implementation.

nodes.name: Hyperspectral Imaging-Based Adulteration Detection of Edible Oil using Optimized Machine Learning Models
nodes.venue: Food Analytical Methods
nodes.abstract: Abstract Oil adulteration poses a significant risk to public health and compromises food quality and authenticity, necessitating reliable and rapid detection methods. This study proposes a non-destructive method for detecting edible oil adulteration using hyperspectral imaging integrated with spectral feature optimization and machine learning techniques. A total of 480 samples, comprising pure oils (tea tree, rose, turmeric, and rosehip oil) and adulterated variants (orange, vitamin E, lemon, and garlic oil), were analyzed using a Specim FX10 camera system. The Savitzky–Golay filter was used to preprocess spectral data, remove noise, and improve spectral smoothness. The spectral features were then optimized and used to train and test various machine learning models, such as Linear Discriminant Analysis, CatBoost, Gradient Boosting Machine, and Extreme Gradient Boosting Machine. The best-performing model among the evaluated models was the Extreme Gradient Boosting Machine, with 99.98% training accuracy, 98.2% testing and validation accuracy, high precision, recall, F1-score, and balanced accuracy (98.3%), Jaccard Index (96.7%), and low log loss (5%) and Hamming loss (2%). The experimental results point to the usefulness of the proposed method in providing accurate, fast, and non-invasive oil adulteration detection. This study indicates the possibility of using hyperspectral imaging with optimized machine learning algorithms to achieve high food quality measurements and real-time applications in the industrial sector of food safety and quality control.

nodes.name: Toward Individualized Digital Twins for Aero-Engines: A Physics-Informed Framework With Fleet-Individual Cross-Attention and Feature Transfer
nodes.venue: Journal of Engineering for Gas Turbines and Power
nodes.abstract: Abstract Digital twin (DT) technology has become a cornerstone for cyber-physical aero-engine systems, enabling full lifecycle digital replication and intelligent management. To address challenges of model adaptability and generalization under restricted access to fleet data conditions, this article proposes a physics-informed DT modeling framework integrating fleet feature transfer and a fleet-individual cross-attention fusion mechanism. The framework is composed of three main components: (1) a physics-embedded network, where a long short-term memory network captures temporal component dynamics, coupled with a multicomponent attention module to model intercomponent interactions; (2) a fleet-individual cross-attention module designed to extract interactive features between individual engines and the entire fleet; and (3) a pretraining and fine-tuning strategy that transfers generalized knowledge from fleet-level models to individual engines, enabling fast deployment without relying on large-scale historical data. Validation on thrust and exhaust gas temperature (EGT) prediction demonstrates superior accuracy and robustness, achieving the lowest mean absolute percentage errors (MAPEs) of 0.23% for thrust and 2.47% for EGT. Compared with baselines (a general fleet model and individual models without fleet features), the proposed approach reduces average MAPE by 47.80–75.49% (thrust) and 4.43–15.91% (EGT), improving both precision and stability. This framework enhances the scalability and digital management efficiency of aero-engine DT systems.

nodes.name: Journal of Engineering for Gas Turbines and Power
Beyond the visible lesion: mycotoxin attenuation and spatial heterogeneity in maize cobs
nodes.venue: Mycotoxin Research
nodes.abstract: Abstract Visible mould is widely used as a practical sorting cue in maize, but it remains unclear whether the visible lesion marks the boundary of mycotoxin contamination within an intact cob. This study examined mycotoxin attenuation, spatial heterogeneity, and co-occurrence in visibly mouldy white maize cobs, using measured distances from the visible mould margin. Cobs with visible mould ( n = 35) were sampled for the study. For each cob, the visible mould margin was coded as 0 mm, and adjacent sections were collected at the 50% and 75% points along the measured distance from the lesion boundary to the distal cob tip, resulting in 98 cob-section observations. Mycotoxins, FUMs (FB1, FB2, FB3), deoxynivalenol (DON), zearalenone (ZEA), nivalenol (NIV) and AF (AFB1) were quantified by liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry. Samples with no detectable levels of mycotoxins were replaced with zero, and total FUMs were calculated (FB1 + FB2 + FB3). The visible mould margin accounted for the largest share of the measured toxin burden, accounting for 84.4% of total FUM, 89.4% of DON, 77.8% of ZEA, and 92.2% of NIV. Adjacent sections retained measurable residual mycotoxins, including 15.6% of total FUM, 10.6% of DON, 22.2% of ZEA, and 7.8% of NIV. In full-distance models, DON, ZEA, and NIV declined significantly with distance, whereas total FUM did not show significant monotonic attenuation. The AFB1 was detected in only three cob sections; these detections co-occurred with Fusarium -associated toxins. Co-occurrence analysis showed that adjacent sections frequently remained positive for multiple Fusarium -associated toxin groups, with the FUM + DON + ZEA profile persisting across measured-distance bands. These findings show that visible mould is a useful warning signal but not a reliable toxicological boundary. The results support cob-level rejection or segregation of visibly mouldy cobs before shelling, rather than lesion-level trimming, as a more defensible food-safety control measure.

nodes.name: Breaking GUI Agent Actions: Realistic Adversarial Attacks on Multimodal LLMs
nodes.venue: ACM Transactions on Multimedia Computing, Communications, and Applications
nodes.abstract: Recent progress in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) has enabled GUI agents that interpret interface screenshots and execute natural-language instructions. However, their increasing role in human–computer interaction raises security concerns. Existing work shows that MLLMs are highly sensitive to interface perturbations, yet most attacks assume unrealistic capabilities such as direct access to model-ready inputs. In real deployments, attackers cannot control the screenshot pipeline or the non-differentiable preprocessing operations preceding inference, rendering many prior attacks ineffective. We introduce Realistic Adversarial Attack (RAA) framework that models the complete screenshot-to-prediction pipeline. To address gradient blockage from non-differentiable preprocessing (e.g., resizing and quantization), we develop a dual-branch differentiable preprocessing module that restores gradient flow while remaining faithful to the actual inference path. To improve robustness against query phrasing changes, we further incorporate a task-level semantic variation mechanism that jointly optimizes over paraphrased task variants. Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B-Instruct and GUI-Owl-7B show that RAA consistently outperforms prior attacks, improving attack success rates by an average of 30% under localized perturbations and a 10.7% under global perturbations, while maintaining strong effectiveness against standard defenses such as resizing, compression, and noise. Ablation studies highlight the roles of perturbation region and semantic diversity. Our framework establishes a practical threat model for GUI agents and offers a foundation for future robustness and security research.

nodes.name: ACM Transactions on Multimedia Computing, Communications, and Applications
A Physics‐Informed Two‐Stage Retrieval Method for EMIT Remote Sensing Methane Plumes
nodes.venue: Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres
nodes.abstract: Abstract Hyperspectral satellite missions, particularly EMIT, have revolutionized methane point source monitoring. However, current operational retrieval pipelines typically rely on physically‐based matched filters followed by labor‐intensive manual verification to mitigate high false alarm rates caused by complex background interference. This dependence on human intervention restricts the scalability and efficiency required for rapid, automated global monitoring. To address these limitations, this paper proposes Plume‐Net, a novel Physics‐Informed Guided Two‐Stage Retrieval Method. Unlike conventional approaches, Plume‐Net decouples the task into a “global existence classification” stage and a “local pixel‐level regression” stage to maximize reliability without human‐in‐the‐loop. The core innovation lies in the integration of physical priors with deep learning: In the first stage, a Physics‐Informed Spectral Gating (PISG) module explicitly injects methane spectral absorption knowledge into the network, dynamically recalibrating channel weights to suppress background noise. In the second stage, to overcome the difficulties of regressing sparse, long‐tail plume distributions, we propose a Plume‐Focused Sampling Strategy and an Intensity‐Aware Pixel‐Level Weighted Loss function, forcing the network to prioritize rare but critical high‐concentration signals. Evaluated on real‐world EMIT observations, Plume‐Net achieves an ROC‐AUC of 0.961 in detection and a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 33.33 ppm·m in quantification. By significantly reducing false positives while maintaining high precision, this method offers a robust, fully automated alternative to current semi‐manual retrieval workflows.

nodes.name: Bridging spatial scales in respiratory viral infection
nodes.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
nodes.abstract: Respiratory viruses spread within the host through a combination of local expansion and occasional long-range dissemination that seeds new infection foci. We present LEAP (Lotka-Euler Airway Pathogen model), an analytically tractable within-host model that captures this two-scale process. The model takes the form of an age-dependent branching process and yields a closed-form expression for the exponential growth rate during early infection. Using empirical data to parameterize the model, we find that productive dissemination requires only a small number of successful long-range seeding events per infected cell, with distinct values for SARS-CoV-2 and influenza A virus. LEAP further predicts that, in these well-adapted viruses, interferon-mediated restriction only weakly affects exponential growth, while remaining decisive for poorly adapted pathogens. More broadly, the model provides a flexible framework for experimentally testable predictions of early infection dynamics.

nodes.name: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
The Structure of Reality: Recognition, Necessity, and Physical Prediction
nodes.abstract: A comparison is a physical occurrence. It needs something to compare, an operation that uses both terms, and a state in which its result can matter to what happens next. If the result is measured, the measurement needs a reference. If it is retained, the record needs a carrier. If the operation transfers energy, that energy must appear in the same account. This book asks how much of physical structure is fixed by those demands. Recognition Science begins with the distinctions already exhibited by actual operations and follows their consequences. Its central arguments remove alternatives: a conserved comparison selects a quadratic reading; its residual and reference fix a normalized cost; preservation of additive comparisons, together with a first costly join, fixes golden scaling. A retained linking observation selects three spatial dimensions under its stated realization conditions. Further constructions ask how the resulting source evolves, transfers energy and leaves records. The argument is technical because the alternatives matter. A theorem that selects one cost from a specified class says exactly which other costs fail and why. Changing the class can change the conclusion. A Hamiltonian that acts on a full field carrier establishes more than a finite matrix calculation, while an exact matrix compression remains useful at its own scope. The reader should be able to identify the physical objects, inspect the hypotheses and follow the reason for each conclusion.

nodes.name: Remote sensing applications in solid waste monitoring and management
nodes.venue: Waste Management & Research: The Journal for a Sustainable Circular Economy
nodes.abstract: The rapid growth of solid waste generation carries significant environmental and public health challenges globally. Traditional waste monitoring methods are not cost-effective and are limited in spatial and temporal scope. Remote sensing, encompassing satellite, aerial, and unmanned platforms, has emerged as a transformative approach to identify, monitor, and manage solid waste sites. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of the state-of-the-art in remote sensing applications for solid waste monitoring and management, covering technological developments in the past 2 decades. We examine sensor platforms (optical, hyperspectral, thermal, synthetic aperture radar, light detection and ranging), data processing and machine learning workflows, major application domains (landfill mapping, illegal dumping detection, volumetric assessment, thermal anomaly detection, greenhouse gas monitoring, marine plastic tracking), and integration with geographic information system and IoT (Internet of Things) systems. The present study also evaluates operational successes, methodological challenges, policy implications, and outlines a research roadmap for enhancing the accuracy, scalability, and real-world adoption of remote sensing in waste management.

nodes.name: Waste Management & Research: The Journal for a Sustainable Circular Economy
Reconciling Food and Energy on the Same Land: An Explainable Artificial Intelligence Framework for Agrivoltaic Suitability Mapping
nodes.venue: Firat University Journal of Experimental and Computational Engineering
nodes.abstract: The swift growth of utility-scale solar farms has created fierce competition for agricultural land, especially in countries where prime solar energy sites and productive croplands coincide. Agrivoltaic structures, which incorporate agricultural food and electricity generation on one parcel, are a structural solution to this kind of land-use conflict; yet the question of where such systems should be sited has, to date, been addressed in the literature predominantly through subjective multi-criteria decision making methods. This study develops a fully data-driven and explainable machine learning framework for agrivoltaic site selection, using the province of Konya—Türkiye's grain basket and its largest agricultural region—as a case study. The site selection problem is formulated as a supervised binary classification task in which the geographic inventory of existing solar installations provides the ground-truth labels. Thirteen selected feature spanning climatic, topographic, economic, and socio-environmental dimensions were examined through Pearson correlation, variance inflation factor, and mutual information gain analyses. Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and Extreme Gradient Boosting machine learning algorithms were trained with hyperparameter optimization, and observed performance variations were verified using omnibus Cochran's Q and pairwise McNemar statistical tests. Extreme Gradient Boosting achieved the highest performance (total accuracy: 0.9549, F1 score: 0.9533), followed by Random Forest (0.9390) and Logistic Regression (0.8661). Explainable artificial intelligence analysis, which renders the black-box nature of the models transparent, revealed that the most decisive factors determining agrivoltaic suitability were, respectively, distance to grid lines and global horizontal irradiance (GHI). The findings suggest that the proposed methodology may help minimize conflicts between energy and food security, thereby providing a strategic planning tool that can support progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals (particularly SDGs 7 and 13).

nodes.name: Firat University Journal of Experimental and Computational Engineering
Psychological preparation in multimodal cancer prehabilitation: a systematic review and meta-synthesis of patients’ experiences
nodes.abstract: Introduction: Prehabilitation aims to optimise psychological status, but psychological provision largely addresses existing distress and what preparation for treatment consists of is unclear as prehabilitation services scale up. We asked how patients experience it, what enables or undermines it, and how their circumstances shape what they can use.Methods: We searched CINAHL, MEDLINE and PsycINFO from inception, last searched 22 May 2026, for peer-reviewed English-language qualitative studies of adults’ experiences of multimodal cancer prehabilitation. Eligible programmes combined at least two of exercise, nutrition and psychological support, and either targeted psychological outcomes or included an element with a stated psychological function; measurement alone did not qualify. Two reviewers appraised reports using the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme checklist plus four domains covering staff training, fidelity, adherence and participants’ words. We synthesised findings by meta-ethnography. No external funding. Registered with PROSPERO (CRD42023434123).Results: Seventeen reports (2021-2026), predominantly surgical and from six high-income countries, drew on 14 independent samples and 230 patients. Across three constructs and 12 subthemes, patients experienced psychological preparation as having something to act on, discovering what their bodies could do, understanding and managing what was coming, being taken seriously and kept going, and not being alone. These functions arose through exercise, dietary support and relationships with staff and peers, not only explicitly psychological input. Prehabilitation added to preparations already under way. Relevance, timing, burden and continuity after surgery enabled or undermined preparation, depending on patients’ beliefs, capacity, demands and support networks.Discussion: Evidence came almost entirely from engagers, and staff training, adherence and fidelity were sparsely reported. Psychological preparation did not map onto a discrete component; it arose where what a programme offered matched what a patient could use. Services should build psychological function into how prehabilitation is delivered, who delivers it, and how it is matched to patients.

nodes.name: Prediction of Surface Roughness in Non-Traditional Machining Using Machine Learning Techniques
nodes.venue: International Journal of Creative and Open Research in Engineering and Management
nodes.abstract: Surface roughness decides how a machined part behaves in service. It affects fatigue life, wear, sealing, friction and, in many cases, whether a part is accepted at inspection at all. Non-traditional machining (NTM) processes such as electrical discharge machining, wire EDM, electrochemical machining, laser beam machining, abrasive water jet machining and ultrasonic machining are now routine choices for hard, brittle and geometrically complex parts. Their surface texture, however, comes from thermal, chemical or erosive mechanisms that are stochastic and strongly coupled, so it is hard to predict with classical physics-based models or with simple regression equations. Over the last two decades, machine learning (ML) has become a practical alternative. Artificial neural networks, support vector regression, tree-based ensembles, fuzzy and neuro-fuzzy systems, and more recently deep learning have all been used to map process parameters and sensor signals to roughness values. This paper reviews that body of work. It first outlines the main NTM processes and the way roughness arises in each, then summarises the factors that influence it and the traditional prediction approaches (empirical, statistical and analytical). The discussion then turns to the ML techniques most often applied, a survey of representative studies, a side-by-side comparison of the techniques, and the benefits that ML brings. The review also looks honestly at the obstacles: small datasets, limited transferability, poor interpretability and inconsistent reporting. From this analysis, the main research gaps are identified and directions for future work are proposed, including hybrid physics-informed models, transfer learning, explainable AI and real-time in-process prediction. 1. Keywords Surface roughness; non-traditional machining; machine learning; artificial neural network; support vector regression; random forest; electrical discharge machining; wire EDM; laser machining; abrasive water jet; predictive modelling; Industry 4.0.

nodes.name: International Journal of Creative and Open Research in Engineering and Management
Outbreak Cast-ML: Short-Term Disease Outbreak Analysis and Case Forecasting Using Machine Learning
nodes.venue: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
nodes.abstract: Timely estimation of disease trends can help public-health teams plan testing, staffing, beds, medicines, and community communication. This paper presents OutbreakCast-ML, a reproducible machine-learning workflow for analysing reported outbreak data and producing short-horizon forecasts of daily cases and cumulative burden. The workflow combines data validation, daily incident-case derivation, exploratory visualization, time-ordered validation, and a comparison of a seasonalnaïve baseline, statistical time-series forecasting, and supervised regression models using lagged features. The supplied figures are included as illustrative historical visualizations of COVID-19 trends in India, including daily reported cases, cumulative cases, state-wise counts, and a Prophet-style forecast with trend components. These images are treated as reference graphics rather than evidence of current or independently validated model performance. No new numerical accuracy claim is made because the underlying dataset and model outputs were not provided for independent reproduction. The paper defines an evaluation protocol using MAE, RMSE, MAPE where mathematically appropriate, and predictioninterval coverage. It also discusses data quality, reporting delays, uncertainty, ethical communication, and the need for human review before operational use. The proposed contribution is a transparent end-to-end design that can be implemented and evaluated on public surveillance data and adapted to other infectious-disease settings.

nodes.name: Shubham Sudam Londhe, Mr. M. D. Shinde
International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
Measuring Visual Clutter in AI-Generated Pillar-to-Pillar Automotive Displays: Objective Metrics, Perception, and Search Performance
nodes.venue: Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
nodes.abstract: Large pillar-to-pillar (P2P) displays are replacing traditional instrument clusters, but their visual richness may impair visual search and increase driver distraction. We examined how visual properties of large automotive displays relate to perceived clutter and search performance using subjective, objective, and behavioral measures. Fifty-five participants viewed 18 AI-generated dashboard videos, completed a detection task, and rated clutter, density, overlap, colorfulness, and brightness; corresponding objective metrics were computed from video frames. Subjective density and overlap best predicted clutter, while overlap, edge density, and colorfulness predicted search time. Factor analysis revealed two dimensions, spatial complexity and surface appearance, showing that spatial properties primarily drive clutter perception and that objective metrics can support early-stage interface screening.

nodes.name: Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
Machine learning-based real-time prediction of lighting classes in adaptive road lighting systems
nodes.venue: Lighting Research & Technology
nodes.abstract: This study presents a machine learning-based framework for real-time prediction of road lighting classes in adaptive lighting systems. A field implementation was conducted on Buyukdere Street in Istanbul using two years of traffic and meteorological data. Lighting scenarios were developed in line with EN 13201 standards, and simulations with dimmable LED luminaires ensured compliance with lighting quality requirements. Hourly traffic flow and vehicle speed were predicted using Extreme Gradient Boosting and mapped to appropriate lighting classes via a rule-based matrix. This predictive approach enables the field-installed system to determine the lighting class in advance for each hour rather than after the period has elapsed. Six months of field data were used to validate the approach across seasonal and daily variations. The models achieved R 2 scores of 0.864 and 0.822 for flow and speed predictions, respectively. Predicted lighting classes reached 92.1% and 89.7% agreement with reference classes in two directions. The resulting energy savings closely matched those obtained from measured traffic-based classification, reaching 32.1% compared with non-adaptive M2-level lighting. The results demonstrate the feasibility of data-driven adaptive lighting for energy-efficient urban road operation while meeting the lighting class requirements prescribed by the standard.

nodes.name: Graph-Based Spatial-Velocity Clustering and Tracking of Unlabeled Radar Point Clouds for Autonomous Vehicles with a Novel Temporal Precision Metric
nodes.venue: Transportation Research Record: Journal of the Transportation Research Board
nodes.abstract: Robust and accurate perception of the environment is crucial for autonomous driving systems. Radar sensors offer unique advantages over LiDAR and cameras, such as robustness to adverse weather, long detection range, and instantaneous velocity measurement via the Doppler effect, while being cost-effective. However, radar point clouds present challenges, including sparsity, noise, and ambiguous measurements. In this paper, we propose a graph-based framework for clustering and tracking unlabeled radar point clouds using velocity and spatial information through connected-component analysis. Our approach aggregates multi-sweep radar data into a unified global coordinate frame, enhancing spatial density and temporal continuity. We introduce a centroid-based temporal tracking algorithm that maintains consistent cluster identities across frames and multiple camera views. To objectively evaluate tracking performance, we develop the Multi-Attribute Temporal Consistency Precision (MATC-Precision) metric, which independently assesses temporal consistency using radar cross section and dynamic properties, features orthogonal to the clustering process. Experiments on the nuScenes dataset demonstrated that our method achieved over 80% tracking precision for clusters tracked across three consecutive frames. Qualitative results validated the robustness of our approach in complex urban environments, effectively handling occlusions, multi-camera views, and static and dynamic objects. This framework provides a scalable solution for reliable radar-based perception in autonomous driving.

nodes.name: Transportation Research Record: Journal of the Transportation Research Board
Exploratory Multimodal Machine Learning for Hazard Response Detection in Semi-Automated Rural Driving
nodes.venue: Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
nodes.abstract: Partially automated driving systems require drivers to remain cognitively engaged and prepared to respond to unexpected roadway hazards despite reduced direct vehicle control. In rural driving, low visibility and sudden animal crossings pose unique safety challenges to driver readiness and response capability. This study presents an exploratory multimodal machine learning framework for hazard-response classification under semi-automated rural driving. Using a high-fidelity driving simulator, EEG, eye activity, behavioral, and subjective workload data were acquired under manual and Advanced Driver Assistance System (ADAS)-supported conditions. Pre-hazard event-level features were evaluated using logistic regression, random forest, and multilayer perceptron classifiers with leave-one-subject-out cross-validation. Random Forest achieved the highest mean classification accuracy, although performance was constrained by class imbalance and limited sensitivity to brake events. Feature-importance analysis identified SART situation-awareness score as the most influential feature, followed by NASA-TLX workload, pupil-diameter change, and EEG-derived measures. These findings support multimodal hazard-response classification for future driver-readiness modeling.

nodes.name: Design, Technical Architecture, and Empirical Field Evaluation of a Digital Environmental Health Premises Inspection Model in Kwara State, Nigeria
nodes.venue: Scholarly Journal of Science and Technology Research and Development
nodes.abstract: This study designed, architected, deployed, and empirically evaluated the Digital Environmental Health Inspection System (DEHIS) a context-tailored, four-tier mobile-to-cloud electronic inspection framework engineered for active field operations across Kwara State, Nigeria. A paired crossover method-comparison design was conducted across Ilorin West, Ilorin East, and Ilorin South Local Government Areas (LGAs) involving a census sample of 35 active field Environmental Health Officers (EHOs). DEHIS integrates mobile field data capture via KoboToolbox client software on Android mobile devices, a server-side Express/Node.js middleware synchronization pipeline utilizing Bearer token authentication, and a Supabase PostgreSQL relational database featuring Row-Level Security (RLS) and stored generated columns to automate domain sub-scoring and sanitary classification. Field performance was evaluated through non-parametric Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for paired score agreement, Bland-Altman method comparison limits of agreement, Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) construct evaluations, and Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations (MICE) sensitivity analyses across missing data profiles. DEHIS successfully digitized the 23-item ES1 evaluation tool, establishing a 115-point total compliance scale and an automated dual-condition Sanitary/Not Sanitary classification algorithm. Among 28 complete paired inspections in the primary EHO cohort, overall mean compliance scores demonstrated no statistically significant difference between legacy paper () and digital DEHIS () modes (mean score difference = points, 95% CI: to , ). Bland-Altman analysis revealed a mean bias of points with 95% limits of agreement spanning to points. Multiple imputation sensitivity testing across all 50 paired records confirmed score parity (pooled mean difference = points, 95% CI: to , ). Field evaluation demonstrated dramatic operational efficiency gains: field data capture time decreased by 36.1% (from to minutes per premise, ), while central data synchronization latency dropped from hours to under seconds. User acceptance evaluation () indicated strong overall system acceptance ( out of , ) and high perceived usefulness (, 84.5% agreement). However, facilitating conditions received lower ratings (, 54.9% agreement), driven by cellular network instability and device accessibility constraints. DEHIS establishes a scientifically validated, automated digital inspection architecture that preserves aggregate scoring parity with paper baselines while eliminating reporting latency, enforcing data completeness, and establishing real-time spatial surveillance. Sustainable scaling across urban and rural wards requires institutionalized device provisioning, dedicated cellular data allowances, and resilient offline synchronization protocols.

nodes.name: Scholarly Journal of Science and Technology Research and Development
Data-efficient prediction of rare earth leaching from industrial residues with physics-constrained machine learning
nodes.abstract: Coal ash, mine-water sludge, red mud and phosphogypsum contain rare earth elements, and each new feedstock needs its own leaching recipe. LixaLearn couples a small neural network to closed-form rate laws for four metal hosts (exchange sites, fast-dissolving minerals, slow-dissolving minerals and a locked fraction), with part of the fast host limited by the solubility of its mineral. The network maps bulk chemistry to 17 rate-law parameters, and one to three laboratory test runs on a new feedstock update them. On 175 synthetic feedstocks of seven types, the error on unseen recipes after three test runs was 5.4 percentage points, against 6.7 for tuned gradient boosting and 5.7 for a network without rate laws. The method was then developed on real data in the open. An earlier version failed a pre-registered test on 57 phosphogypsum runs, because its rate laws had no solubility limit; with a solubility-limited host and the common-ion effect of sulfate, three test runs predicted the other runs to 7.4 points, against 10.9 for gradient boosting and 11.5 for the network without rate laws (a development result). In the final held-out test, on 29 runs of an ion-adsorption clay, LixaLearn beat gradient boosting (3.3 against 5.5 points) and the direct network (12.3), but not the mean of the three test runs (2.7), and it did not rank the clay runs. On red mud leached with citric acid, the machine-learning models remained better. Physics-constrained learning transferred to real feedstocks where its rate laws had the right structure, and checking that structure on a few complete runs should come before using it on a new kind of feedstock.

nodes.name: A multi-source earth observation and artificial intelligence framework for unsupervised water-use anomaly screening in Mediterranean agriculture
nodes.venue: Scientific Reports
nodes.abstract: Abstract Reliable screening of agricultural water-use anomalies over large areas remains challenging because verified event labels and field observations are rarely available. We present AI4WaterGuard, a multi-source Earth Observation and artificial intelligence framework for unsupervised water-use anomaly screening across Cyprus. Using 617,862 records from 1,974 centroids across six hydrological years, six primary detector families were assessed under nested temporal cross-validation with training-consistent scaling, validity-aware scoring, and harmonised temporal support. Among the five centroid-sequence detectors, the convolutional neural network autoencoder showed the strongest response to the strong-reference controlled synthetic proxy, achieving Average Precision of $$0.893\pm 0.130$$ and Proxy F1 of $$0.880\pm 0.100$$ . The spatially explicit convolutional long short-term memory variational autoencoder was evaluated at finer land-pixel-sequence granularity and interpreted descriptively. Across five perturbation patterns and three severities, the convolutional neural network autoencoder achieved an equal-scenario mean Average Precision of 0.342, declining to 0.088 for weak perturbations. These synthetic metrics quantify controlled-proxy sensitivity, not field-validated detection performance. Operational post-processing on 1,157 WorldCover-eligible centroids combined threshold sensitivity, 1,000 exact-count randomisations, a primary Top-50 inspection-prioritisation queue with a nested Top-20 high-priority subset, and common-cadence spatiotemporal events. The resulting screening priorities require independent administrative and field evidence to establish physical cause or legal status.

nodes.name: <b>Interpretable Deep Learning for Retinal Disease Detection</b>
nodes.venue: Asian Journal of Electrical and Electronic Engineering
nodes.abstract: Eye diseases are a leading cause of global vision impairment, yet detection is often hindered by limited resources and geographic barriers. While Deep Learning (DL) offers automated diagnostic solutions, its black-box nature challenges clinical trust. This research investigates whether interpretability can be integrated into DL models for eye disease classification without compromising performance. Using an EfficientNet-B0 architecture, two models were trained on fundus images: one trained only on real images and another incorporating synthetic images generated by a Deep Convolutional Generative Adversarial Network (DCGAN) to simulate insufficient data. Both training approaches were evaluated using 3-fold cross-validation and analysed with eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques: Grad-CAM for visual heatmaps and SHAP for feature-contribution insights. A General Practitioner (GP) also assessed the clinical relevance of selected Grad-CAM outputs. Cross-validation produced mean accuracies of 91.59% ± 0.81% for the real-only model and 90.51% ± 0.83% for the mixed model, with no statistically significant difference in accuracy (paired t-test, p = 0.366). Synthetic image quality was further evaluated using fidelity and diversity metrics, while additional analyses examined classification errors, calibration, and robustness to explanations. These results demonstrate the feasibility of integrating interpretability with DL models for retinal disease classification, including scenarios involving synthetic data augmentation, supporting further development of transparent and accurate automated medical diagnostic tools.

Artificial Intelligence in Multimodal Neuroimaging Research on Depression: A Bibliometric Analysis
nodes.venue: Psychiatry Investigation
nodes.abstract: Objective To conduct a systematic bibliometric review of artificial intelligence (AI)-based multimodal neuroimaging research in depression, mapping its evolution, collaborative networks, and intellectual foundations to guide future translation.Methods Records were retrieved from Web of Science Core Collection (search date: 1 September 2025) using terms for depression, neuroimaging modalities, and AI/machine learning (ML)/deep learning. English, peer-reviewed articles/reviews (2001–2025) were screened; 1,232 studies were retained after deduplication and filtering. Analyses included annual output trends, co-authorship networks (countries/institutions/authors), keyword co-occurrence clustering with burst detection, and co-citation/bibliographic coupling using VOSviewer (v1.6.20) and Bibliometrix (v4.5.1).Results Annual publications rose from <20/year to 202 in 2024; 2025 counts (n=173) reflect January–August only. The international network spans 42 countries/regions linked by 320 co-authorship ties (total link strength=1,228; density of approximately 0.37). USA, China, and the UK constitute the epistemic core, with expanding participation from India, Brazil, and Iran. Institutional and author overlays indicate a small-world, hierarchical organization (205 institutions; 10 collaboration communities; author network 168 researchers) characterized by a productive core and long tail. Six keyword clusters delineate a functional workflow: 1) biomarkers/phenotypes, 2) functional connectivity, 3) machine-learning/computational approaches, 4) multimodal/precision psychiatry, 5) diagnostic classification/algorithm development, and 6) structural imaging/comorbidity. Co-citation and coupling reveal a progression from early ML and connectivity foundations to deep/graph models, multimodal fusion, explainability, and treatment-oriented prediction.Conclusion AI-based multimodal neuroimaging in depression has evolved into a coherent, translationally focused field. Current trends emphasize model validation, interpretability, and cross-site generalization, supported by expanding international collaboration. Future priorities include harmonized data sharing, explainable modeling, and theory-informed clinical translation.

nodes.name: TSE-Net: Semi-supervised monocular height estimation from single remote sensing images
nodes.venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
nodes.abstract: Monocular height estimation plays a critical role in 3D perception for remote sensing, offering a cost-effective alternative to multi-view or LiDAR-based methods. While deep learning has significantly advanced the capabilities of monocular height estimation, these methods remain fundamentally limited by the availability of labeled data, which are expensive and labor-intensive to obtain at scale. The scarcity of high-quality annotations hinders the generalization and performance of existing models. To overcome this limitation, we propose leveraging large volumes of unlabeled data through a semi-supervised learning framework, enabling the model to extract informative cues from unlabeled samples and improve its predictive performance. In this work, we introduce Teacher-Student-Exam Network (TSE-Net), a self-training pipeline for semi-supervised monocular height estimation. The pipeline integrates teacher, student, and exam networks. The student network is trained on unlabeled data using pseudo-labels generated by the teacher network, while the exam network functions as a temporal ensemble of the student network to stabilize performance. The teacher network is formulated as a joint regression and classification model: the regression branch predicts height values that serve as pseudo-labels, and the classification branch predicts height value classes along with class probabilities, which are used to filter pseudo-labels. Height value classes are defined using a novel Hierarchical Bi-Cut (HBC) strategy to address the inherent long-tailed distribution of heights, and the predicted class probabilities are calibrated with a Plackett-Luce model to reflect the expected accuracy of pseudo-labels. We evaluate the proposed pipeline on three datasets spanning different resolutions and imaging modalities: the ISPRS Vaihingen dataset (IR-R-G aerial images, 0.09 m resolution), the SynRS3D dataset (synthetic images, 0.6–1 m resolution), and the GBH dataset (satellite RGB images, 3 m resolution). Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms supervised and semi-supervised baselines in low-label regimes, and ablation studies confirm the contribution and dataset-dependent behavior of each design component. Code is available at https://github.com/zhu-xlab/tse-net . • First self-training-based semi-supervised learning pipeline for monocular height estimation. • Teacher-Student-Exam pipeline with classification-regression teacher. • Hierarchical Bi-Cut reduces long-tailed biases in height predictions. • Plackett-Luce model aligns pseudo-label reliability with class confidence. • Up to 29.07% gap reduction between 100% and 0.1% labeled data.

Role of Artificial Intelligence and IoT in Pest Monitoring
nodes.abstract: Pests remain a major threat to crop production, and pest monitoring has changed considerably with the development of new technologies. This chapter examines how artificial intelligence and the Internet of Things have combined to transform pest monitoring, shifting it from manual field scouting to continuous sensor-driven surveillance. It starts with the sensing platforms like satellites, drones, and ground-based wireless sensor networks that now supply the images and environmental readings on which detection depends. It then runs through machine learning and deep learning models, especially convolutional neural networks and detection frameworks such as YOLO, trained to spot pests and the damage they cause. The role of the Internet of Things is explored through wireless sensors, edge and fog computing, and cloud platforms that keep this intelligence connected to the field, along with newer ideas like federated learning and digital twins are also discussed for improving data handling, system reliability, and real-time decision-making. This chapter highlights practical applications of these technologies in orchards, greenhouses, and open-field conditions, while also discussing challenges related to data availability, energy requirements, connectivity, and standardization. Overall, the integration of AI and IoT offers a promising approach for developing more efficient, timely, and reliable pest monitoring systems that can support better pest management at the farm level. Keywords: Artificial intelligence; Internet of Things; AIoT; Pest monitoring; Remote sensing; Deep learning; Precision agriculture.

nodes.name: RSAA-UNet: A Residual Squeeze-and-Excitation Attention U-Net with Atrous Context and Focal-Tversky Supervision for Lower-Grade Glioma Segmentation on FLAIR MRI under a Patient-Wise Evaluation Protocol
nodes.venue: IJARCCE
nodes.abstract: Outlining lower-grade glioma (LGG) on FLAIR MRI is a prerequisite for volumetric follow-up and radiogenomic work, yet many published U-Net pipelines for the public TCGA-LGG collection do not state, or do not enforce, a clean separation of patients between training and testing.This paper describes RSAA-UNet, a 2-D encoderdecoder that combines residual double-convolution blocks, squeeze-and-excitation (SE) recalibration, additive attention gates on all four skip connections, an atrous spatial pyramid pooling (ASPP) module at the bottleneck, and deep supervision at three decoder levels, trained with a Focal-Tversky plus binary cross-entropy objective.Ten networks (three baselines, two RSAA-UNet variants and five single-component ablations) were trained under one protocol on a patient-wise 78/16/16 split of 110 patients (3,929 slices) and evaluated on 16 unseen patients (498 slices, 182 containing tumour).Flip-based test-time augmentation and small-component removal were examined as inference options.On tumour-containing slices the full RSAA-UNet with both inference steps reached a Dice coefficient of 0.715 (patient-bootstrap 95% CI 0.651-0.771),against 0.714 for U-Net and 0.743 for the strongest baseline, a residual U-Net; no difference was significant at the patient level after Holm correction.The proposed objective lowered the falsepositive rate on tumour-free slices to 2.5%, compared with 4.4-6.0%for the baselines, and the ablation pointed to residual connections and SE recalibration as the most useful components, while attention gates and ASPP gave no measurable benefit here.Training of the full model also diverged after epoch 20, so its weights come from an early checkpoint.The Discussion explains why a strict patient-wise protocol gives lower Dice values than those usually quoted for this dataset, compares the results with five published studies, and lists the changes needed before the architecture can be judged conclusively.

nodes.name: Machine learning approaches to predict health facility delivery among reproductive-age women in East Africa
nodes.venue: Scientific African
nodes.abstract: Delivery at health facilities offer access to emergency obstetric care and guarantee handling of problems like eclampsia, postpartum hemorrhage, and obstructed labor. Using machine learning to predict delivery at a health facility supports automated decision-making, enhances classification accuracy, and scales well when dealing with large and complex datasets. The aim of this research was to predict health facility delivery among women of reproductive age in East Africa by applying a machine-learning approach. A cross-sectional study design was used, drawing on Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) datasets from 11 East African countries collected between 2015 and 2024. Data preprocessing involved cleaning, transformation, and integration, along with one-hot encoding, 80/20% data splitting, and 10-fold stratified cross-validation. Four machine-learning algorithms were assessed, such as random forest, decision tree, k-nearest neighbors, and Naïve Bayes. The random forest classifier achieved the highest performance, yielding an area under the curve (AUC) of 84.8% and an accuracy of 82.9%. Shapley Additive exPlanation (SHAP)-based feature importance analysis identified wealth index, women’s and husbands’ educational status, number of children, place of residence, distance to health facility, and frequency of Antenatal Care (ANC) visits as the strongest predictors of health facility delivery. These results offer actionable insights for planners, Non-Governmental Organizations (NGOs), and policymakers to design targeted and culturally appropriate interventions that improve equitable access to maternal health services. Future studies should test advanced models such as ensemble and deep learning, integrate geospatial and health system data, and develop secure real-time predictive tools within national health platforms.

nodes.name: Entropy guided spectral phenological feature engineering using Sentinel-2A data for Pan-Arctic vegetation classification
nodes.venue: Scientific Reports
nodes.abstract: Arctic vegetation plays a critical role in regulating terrestrial ecosystem structure and function. Existing remote-sensing classification products are often limited in thematic detail and accuracy because of the region’s inaccessibility and the underuse of high-dimensional spectral and phenological information. This study established a Pan-Arctic vegetation classification system comprising Barren Tundra (BT), Sparse Tundra (ST), Cyperaceae Tundra (CT), Graminoid Tundra (GT), Wet Tundra (WT), Grass, and Shrub. A total of 161 homogeneous samples were selected across the Pan-Arctic domain through multi-source consistency filtering and visual verification. These samples were used for spectral–phenological feature development, entropy-based feature evaluation, threshold definition, and model construction. We introduced spectral characteristic information entropy (SCIE) and spectral characteristic information weight coefficients (SCIWC) to characterize spectral information content and relative feature importance. The entropy-guided feature set improved inter-class separability; for example, green-band information helped distinguish BT from ST, whereas red-band information contributed to the separation of CT and GT. Final map accuracy was assessed independently using 761 reference points in Yamal’skiy Rayon, which were not used for feature development or model construction. The classification achieved an overall accuracy of 90.67% and a Kappa coefficient of 0.88. A comparison with CALC-2020 indicated broad spatial consistency, while differences reflected the finer thematic detail and differing class definitions of the two products. These results demonstrate the potential of entropy-guided spectral–phenological feature engineering for fine-scale Arctic vegetation mapping, while further multi-region and multi-year validation is needed to assess Pan-Arctic transferability.

nodes.name: Demographics-Informed Neural Network for Multimodal Spatiotemporal Forecasting of Urban Growth and Travel Patterns Using Satellite Imagery
nodes.venue: Journal of Transportation Engineering Part A Systems
nodes.abstract: Abstract Transportation planning requires anticipating how built environments, population characteristics, and aggregate travel indicators evolve over time. Conventional forecasting approaches often treat these dimensions separately, limiting their ability to represent spatial-demographic change. This study introduces the Demographics-Informed Neural Network (DINN), a deep learning framework that forecasts next-year county-level satellite imagery from historical image sequences while enforcing demographic consistency through a frozen demographic predictor. DINN combines an encoder-decoder image predictor, gated skip connections, demographic bottleneck fusion, and demographic consistency regularization. The frozen demographic encoder is then reused as a fixed feature extractor to estimate aggregate county-level commute-mode and vehicle-availability indicators. Experiments using US county data from 2012 to 2023 show that DINN achieves an MSE of 0.00379 and SSIM of 0.8342 for satellite image prediction. Across repeated grouped spatial splits, DINN provides modest but consistent improvements over ConvLSTM, transformer-based, and encoder-decoder baselines, with stronger performance on both image reconstruction and change-detection metrics. The demographic predictor explains approximately 80% of the variance in population characteristics from satellite imagery. Transfer learning results show higher accuracy for absolute travel-indicator counts than for scale-controlled shares, indicating that part of the signal reflects county population scale. Overall, the findings suggest that satellite-derived spatial representations capture built-environment and demographic correlates of aggregate travel indicators; however, the results should be interpreted as county-level predictive associations rather than causal behavioral inference.

Deep Learning-Based Object Detection for Fashion, Uniform, and PPE Items: A Systematic Literature Review
nodes.venue: Journal of Information Systems and Informatics
nodes.abstract: Deep learning-based object detection for clothing and uniform items spans two research streams: fashion and apparel detection for e-commerce, and personal protective equipment (PPE) compliance detection for occupational safety. No prior review has jointly synthesized these streams with a detection-centric scope. This study addresses that gap through a PRISMA 2020-guided systematic literature review of 1,378 records from Scopus as the sole database, identified via two Boolean queries and screened for object detection or instance segmentation of clothing, uniform, or PPE items, yielding 26 empirical studies published between 2021 and 2026. One-stage YOLO-based detectors dominate the corpus (18 of 26 studies, up to 96.9% mAP50 at 7.3 ms inference), a dominance partly attributable to an architectural constraint in the PPE-domain search query; two-stage R-CNN and transformer-based architectures remain comparatively underexplored, the latter represented by only two studies. Dataset scale is markedly asymmetric between public fashion benchmarks (up to 491,895 images) and PPE-specific collections (as few as 1,330 images), though an emerging benchmark-reuse pattern partly offsets this gap within the PPE domain. This review contributes a cross-domain synthesis benchmarked against five prior reviews, an explicit architecture-dataset-metric mapping, a proposed nine-element minimum reporting standard, and a challenge taxonomy that surfaces previously undiscussed ethical and cultural-representation gaps in this literature

Attacking visual foundation depth estimation model with adaptable adversarial patch
nodes.venue: Scientific Reports
nodes.abstract: Vision foundation models (VFMs) have demonstrated strong generalization ability across various downstream tasks and scenes. However, their vulnerability to adversarial examples, particularly in safety-critical applications, remains insufficiently understood. This paper investigates the attack effect of physical adversarial patches on monocular depth estimation (MDE) models, specifically the foundation model Depth Anything, widely used in fields such as autonomous driving and robotic navigation. First, we introduce a universal patch attack pipeline and present the following key observations: 1) Attack effectiveness : In the pixel-wise dense prediction task of MDE, adversarial effects are largely confined to the patch area and do not spread to other regions, indicating that foundation models have enhanced adversarial robustness compared to traditional models. 2) Attack interpretability : The learned adversarial patches often contain semantically meaningful content, such as forests or buildings, leading to corresponding erroneous depth predictions, which adds interpretability to the attack’s behavior. Based on the observations, we focus on improving the applicability of adversarial patches in real-world environments by proposing a plug-and-play augmentation method, termed MixCrop, that enhances attack effectiveness, especially when patch semantics are incomplete or repetitive. Extensive experiments including physical attacks demonstrate that the patched objects can effectively vanish from the predicted depth map. The learned patches also have strong generalization ability across various objects and scenes.

nodes.name: An improved polarization-sensitive semi-analytic monte carlo simulation method for bathymetric lidar considering complex water-column stratification
nodes.venue: Scientific Reports
nodes.abstract: Bathymetric lidar simulation has long treated seawater as an optically uniform medium, so existing models cannot reproduce how a thermocline, a turbidity layer, or a subsurface chlorophyll maximum reshapes the polarized echo. This paper develops an improved polarization-sensitive semi-analytic Monte Carlo (SMC) method for vertically stratified water. Earlier semi-analytic treatments either keep the polarization state but collapse the column to a homogeneous medium, or resolve the vertical structure but carry only a scalar photon weight; here the photon engine itself is rebuilt around layer-aware free-path marching and a layer-resolved local estimate, the forced-scoring weight is rederived so that it remains unbiased where the attenuation coefficient and the Mueller matrix change discontinuously, and the full Stokes state is carried through every scattering event. Importance sampling, adaptive step control near boundaries, and a GPU-mapped multiple-scattering synthesis keep the cost within reach of parameter sweeps. Against an analytic small-angle solution the method agrees to better than 1% inside the quasi-single-scattering window where that solution is valid, and against a converged conventional Monte Carlo reference it holds waveform and degree-of-polarization errors below 1% at roughly a tenth of the photon budget. Under stratified scenes it reproduces the layer-specific pulse broadening, peak delay, and co- and cross-polarized depolarization signatures that homogeneous models cannot generate. Reading the two polarization channels jointly reduces the stratification-induced bottom-detection bias from about 0.34 m to about 0.10 m once the waveform signal-to-noise ratio exceeds 25 dB, and it supports a preliminary retrieval of layer depth and optical contrast, although absorption and scattering remain strongly correlated. The evidence is entirely numerical, and the flat-layer geometry, the static sea surface, the neglect of wave-facet refraction, and the absence of any comparison with field-measured airborne waveforms bound what can be claimed from it.
